name: The Squire's Walking Stick

location.address: Tullynally Castle demesne, Pakenham Hall Road, Castlepollard, Co. Westmeath (left of the main avenue on the way out)

official_register.name: Heritage Trees of Ireland (Tree Council of Ireland, NBDC dataset 27), record 501, 'Named trees' (probable match)

access: Estate-owned. Tullynally says the parkland with its magnificent trees is open to walkers, dogs on leads, throughout the year. The gardens (EUR 9 adult) are open 21 March to 27 September 2026, Thursday to Sunday 9am to 5pm (daily in Heritage Week). The estate's trail places this tree on the left of the main avenue on the way out; whether that stretch is inside the ticketed garden or free parkland is not stated, so ask at reception.
transport: Castlepollard 2 km; Mullingar about 25 km. No public transport verified.
verify_notes: Tullynally's own tree trail (fetched; item 11): a young oak was bred from 'the tallest in the demesne, the Squire's Walking Stick, which you can see on the left of the main avenue on the way out'. Irish Times profile of Thomas Pakenham ('Branching out', fetched): 'The Tullynally Oak, known as the Squire's Walking Stick, is the tallest oak in the Republic.' Yahoo Style / Telegraph piece on private arboretums (fetched): 'the tallest oak in Ireland at 112ft, planted by the 1st Baron Longford in 1745'. The 1745 date has one source only and the Irish Times says 'Republic', the Telegraph says 'Ireland': state the tallest claim as 'reported'. 112 ft = 34 m. Heritage Trees register record 501 is the only 'Named trees' Quercus robur at Tullynally (150-200 years in 2009, pin 53.68659,-7.32262, Irish Grid conversion, about 100 m); CONFLICT: the band implies about 170-220 years now, against 1745 (about 280). So age is shown broad 200-280 and the match to record 501 is probable, not proved; the pin is for the writer to treat as site-level. Alive: no dated photo of the tree; the 2025-26 Telegraph piece speaks of it in the present tense; lifecheck NONE at the pin. Pakenham's book 'In the Company of Trees' (2015) is the family's own writing about the demesne. Recognition line candidate: the tall straight oak beside the main avenue, noticeably taller than the other oaks.
